endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: ID.DE-P2: Data processing ecosystem parties (e.g., service providers, customers, partners, product manufacturers, application developers) are identified, prioritized, and assessed using a privacy risk assessment process.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Apply TEVV practices for content provenance (e.g., probing a system's synthetic data generation capabilities for potential misuse or vulnerabilities.

endorsements.title: FUTURE-AI: international consensus guideline for trustworthy and deployable artificial intelligence in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Prioritise all the risks depending on their likelihood and consequences

endorsements.title: Integrating enterprise risk management to address AI-related risks in healthcare: Strategies for effective risk mitigation and implementation
endorsements.issuer: Journal of healthcare risk management : the journal of the American Society for Healthcare Risk Management
endorsements.quote: Mapping these risks and prioritizing them based on a scale of probability and impact is crucial for developing appropriate mitigation strategies.

endorsements.title: ONRAMP-AI-VRAR: an operational protocol for ethics and governance of AI-enabled immersive psychotherapy
endorsements.quote: Rate harms by likelihood and impact, with categories for simulation sickness, re-traumatization, privacy breaches, etc.

commentary.bottom_line: Five sources endorse rating AI risks by likelihood and impact, but no study has tested whether doing so changes response planning or patient outcomes, and no study documents the hazard of unprioritized risks being ignored. Health systems adopting this practice would be relying on expert consensus and borrowed risk-management convention rather than measured effect.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice and none documents the hazard, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. Of the five endorsements, three (FUTURE-AI, the enterprise risk management commentary, and ONRAMP-AI-VRAR) state the likelihood-and-impact rule directly. The CHAI and NIST excerpts address privacy party assessment and content provenance testing, which bear on the recommendation only indirectly.

Likelihood-by-impact scoring comes from general risk management, but no supplied study shows that it helps teams catch AI errors before they reach patients. The ONRAMP-AI-VRAR protocol lists harms such as re-traumatization and privacy breaches, which suggests severity categories may need to be specific to each clinical setting. That idea remains untested.

The endorsing sources are voluntary frameworks, consensus guidance, and commentaries. None of the supplied material cites a statute or binding rule that requires likelihood-and-impact rating of AI risks. Adoption would therefore rest on alignment with the NIST and CHAI frameworks rather than on a compliance mandate.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares AI deployments that used structured likelihood-and-impact rating with deployments that did not, whether the outcome is completeness of response plans, time to mitigation, or patient harm. No study measures how often identified AI risks go unaddressed when no one ranks them. Studies are also needed on inter-rater agreement for likelihood and impact scores when teams assess AI tools, because the value of prioritization depends on whether scores are consistent across assessors.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The endorsements do not say whether impact ratings should weigh harms that fall unevenly on these groups. A scoring scheme built on average impact could rank risks concentrated in small or underserved populations as low priority, and that possibility has not been examined.
